bibliography.abstract: The process of urbanization is accompanied by alterations in the urban climate behavior, and this in turn is characterized by spatial-temporal variations in temperature that are related to the urban and environmental characteristics of the city. In this context, urban morphology and vegetation are a strategy for reducing the impact of microclimate during periods of high temperature. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between summer surface temperature and urban design characteristics in residential areas of the Renca district, which is in the northwest of the city of Santiago. The use of summer LANDSAT satellite imagery (2013–2021) and thermal and multispectral UAVs (Mavic enterprise dual and Phantom 4, respectively) provided detailed information about surface temperature at local and micro scale, with Landsat characterising the average thermal behaviour of local climate zones and UAV observations resolving fine-scale variability within representative residential scenarios, so that the two datasets offer complementary spatial and temporal perspectives on the same phenomenon. At local scale, the LANDSAT results show that climate zones are related to surface temperature. More compact residential areas, industrial zones and areas with paved or bare soils are the warmest. At micro-scale a series of urban scenarios were evaluated by means of urban and environmental descriptors that were related to surface temperature data. The results obtained have contributed to the identification of factors that explain climate behavior at the micro-scale. These factors include a direct relationship between temperature and sky view factor, and an inverse relationship with respect to vegetation (NDVI) and height-to-width ratio. Surface temperatures ranged from 13 °C to 47 °C across the commune, and a difference of about 7 °C was observed between UAV-derived (40.3 °C) and Landsat-derived (33.6 °C) average temperatures. These findings provide actionable inputs for climate-sensitive urban design and planning guidelines.

en.caveats: The micro-scale observational data is drawn exclusively from representative residential scenarios within a single municipality in Santiago.
en.what: The authors combined summer Landsat satellite imagery from 2013 to 2021 with thermal and multispectral drone flights to evaluate micro-scale surface temperatures across residential scenarios in Renca, a northwest district of Santiago, Chile. Surface temperatures ranged from 13 °C to 47 °C across the municipality, with drone sensors capturing higher average temperatures (40.3 °C) than Landsat observations (33.6 °C). Higher surface temperatures correlated directly with larger sky view factors and inversely with vegetation density (NDVI) and building height-to-street width ratios.
en.why: The findings quantify a 7 °C discrepancy between coarse satellite measurements and high-resolution drone readings, demonstrating how spatial resolution alters the observed thermal performance of specific residential designs.
